2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
Benelli Showed the World Its New Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept at EICMA 2026 and It's a Triple!
43 photos
Photo: Benelli Motorcycles
I tend to avoid seeing “signs” in life. Some people might interpret them that way, but I typically try to find the logical explanation behind it all. It can be entertaining to get caught up in that sort of thought process, though, even for just a little bit. Let me explain.
A few weeks ago I stumbled across my old collection of motorcycle magazines. A German publisher had released them on the market over 20 years ago, and I’ve been happy to take good care of them since. I only took one out of the drawer, thinking I’d re-read them all within a few weeks. I’m still stuck in nostalgia mode since, and even took photos of the bikes inside to show them to my buddy Omar (who was probably still in kindergarten back in 2003).
One event led to another, and I somehow remembered one of my junior-high “sweethearts”: the Benelli Tornado Tre 900 (Novecento). It was my first time falling in love with a bike that had an inline-three cylinder engine. To me, it felt even more exclusive and exciting than a Ducati or an Aprilia , although the latter also commanded part of my attention with its V4 engines. Drifting shifted my focus from bikes to cars for a few years, and I had almost forgotten about he Tornado Tre 900 until last month.
Well, at least I haven’t thought about it for a long time. As I knew that my colleague, Cristian Curmei, would embark on his first-ever trip to EICMA in Italy, I asked him to keep me updated about the show and maybe even get in touch with a few of the top manufacturers for some test rides in 2027. He has been at it for a few days, but I just didn’t find the time to sit down and look through photos.
It all changed when I got a glimpse of what just happened at the Benelli stand. First of all, the Italian manufacturer used the show as a platform to reveal its new brand identity. But the main event had three motorcycles sitting under the covers, with Mr. Roberto Vitali (Europe Sales, Marketing and Communication Director, Benelli) and Mr. Marco Belluci (Technical and R&D Director, Benelli) walking us through the secrets inside.
Photo: Cristian Curmei for autoevolution Cristian was fortunate enough to also hear from Mr. Stefano Casanova (Chief Designer) during a short interview, and I genuinely didn’t expect Benelli to make such a bold move at EICMA this year. The Tornado 550 launched earlier this year seemed like an interesting proposition, but I tend to be highly wary of anything that’s powered by a parallel twin engine as I’m too nostalgic about the “good old days” to appreciate what these units can achieve.
Two of the motorcycles on the podium were the Tornado Naked Twin 700 and the TRK 602 X, and I might see what they’re like next year. However, the main star of the show was the Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept which marks the return of Benelli’s three-cylinder motor. This all feels like a teaser for the future, and the manufacturer calls this bike a “test bed” for the ideas its currently developing.
We’re certainly looking at a bold design here, and it almost reminded me of the AMB 001 for a second. Information is scarce at the moment, but we do know that displacement is up to almost 900 cc and the engine itself will only weigh 123 lbs/56 kg. If you’ll ever get to ride one, the rev limit comes on at 14,000 rpm which should make for one hell of a soundtrack.
Whether this bike will become reality or “transfer” is capabilities to a different model or not, riders will have access to all the modern amenities you can expect from a premium motorcycle including ride-by-wire throttle control, a slipper clutch and bidirectional quickshifter, and a six-axis IMU (inertial measurement unit). I wouldn’t say that’s the most exciting part of the story.
Photo: Benelli Having the exhaust integrated in the rear section feels like an interesting approach, solving a design problem some riders may have complained about in the past, but also likely making it impossible to ever have a passenger ride pillion with you. I guess most people wouldn’t even think about something like that in the first place, at least not with this kind of motorcycle.
Think fully-adjustable Ohlins suspension on the rear, and Marzocchi up-front, an aluminum swingarm with an inverted design, and slick tires (which obviously won’t make it into the final, road-going product). Looking at the pictures it feels the design team has done a good job integrating the air intake into the fascia. I’m certain some of you will be thrilled about the IMU-controlled active aero, and I admit it’s a pretty cool trick.
Since MotoGP has banned active aero devices, this is one way to brag about having access to superior technology. It genuinely feels like an arms race between manufacturers to come up with the wildest tech imaginable, and it’s great to know that the winglets are independently controlled. The system will look at the riding conditions, the speed and your inputs to analyze how and when to deploy them, and it should technically help riders be faster and safer at the same time.
Photo: Benelli To me, the most interesting part about the Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept is that it features a modular frame, which is a sure sign Benelli is planning to expand the line-up with multiple models soon. We’ve seen this approach in the automotive industry, but I can’t recall a wide scale application in the motorcycle sector. Benelli sees this as the opportunity for the frame to adapt to the motorcycle and not the other way around.
The three independent modules (aluminum front and rear, central section from composite material) bring flexibility into the equation, which could also lower development and manufacturing costs while potentially opening up a whole new world for customization. I’ll definitely have to look into it all soon. If I get to ride this bike, I might have to start believing in signs.

2026 SEMA Show • This Batmobile-Looking Lamborghini Temerario Is on Display at SEMA
Rare McLaren Speedtail With 54 Miles Hits the “Used” Car Market Stateside
11 photos
Photo: Instagram | mph
This ultra-rare and ultra-hot McLaren Speedtail is searching for a new home in the United States of America as we speak, and you should definitely keep reading if you want to spruce up your high-end car collection with one of these, because only 106 of them were made.
The production number is actually a reference to the iconic McLaren F1, because that’s how many were made between 1992 and 1998. The Speedtail was assembled at the Woking factory, in England, in 2020, and just like its spiritual predecessor, it also features a three-seat layout, with the driver sitting in the center and slightly forward of the two passengers. The seating layout may be unconventional, but it provides better visibility, not to mention more driving engagement.
McLaren’s Speedtail is the brand’s fourth installment in the Ultimate Series, after the F1, the P1, and the Senna, though some believe that the latter model should not be on this list for different reasons that were discussed years ago when it broke cover. It is a two-door coupe with a carbon fiber monocoque, and the passenger seats have been integrated into the chassis. And despite the fact that it came out six years ago, the Speedtail does not yet have a modern-day equivalent.
Well, unless you count the W1, which is a proper hypercar, whereas the Speedtail is more of an exotic grand tourer. The McLaren Speedtail shares numerous nuts and bolts not only with the demised 720S, but also the Elva and the Senna. It features a teardrop-shaped inspired design to minimize drag, and benefits from a lot of carbon fiber. Electrochromic glass is on deck, and as you likely remember, this is a multi-million dollar machine.
Photo: Instagram | mph When it first came out, it was offered from the equivalent of roughly $2.2 million, and that is pretty much how much it still costs today . For instance, an example fetched over $2.2 million back in August 2026, during an online auction, and it had 231 miles (372 km) on the odo. A few months before, another car, this time with 74 miles (119 km), fetched almost $2.1 million, and at the beginning of 2026, one sold for just under $2 million, with 216 miles (347 km).
Therefore, your pockets must be really deep if you plan on sprucing up your high-end car collection with one of these, but that’s not a surprise, is it? Now, after refreshing our memory, it is time to proceed to the real reason behind this story, which is the McLaren Speedtail pictured in the gallery. You are looking at car #93, according to the vendor, @mph on Instagram, and it is finished in blue, on top of a beige/tan and black interior.
As mentioned in the title, this very rare machine has only 54 miles (87 km) under its belt, and the selling dealer behind it mentioned several things in the ad. These include the MSO exterior, the advanced aerodynamics, nose-lift system, as well as the central diving position that we already told you about, and a few other features.
Photo: Instagram | mph The powertrain is something that we haven’t discussed yet, but as you likely remember, it features an upgraded version of the 4-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine found on the 720S. The mill, however, is assisted by electricity, and is officially rated at 1,036 brake horsepower (1,050 ps/772 kW) and 848 pound-feet (1,150 Nm) of torque. The model is rear-wheel drive, and takes just 12.8 seconds to sprint from 0 to 186 mph (0 to 300 kph). Keep the right pedal pinned to the floor, and it will max out at 250 mph (403 kph).
Due to the unique look, three-seat interior layout with the driver flanked by the passengers and sitting in front of them, the jaw-dropping amount of power, the impressive performance, and the fact that you have more chances of encountering a unicorn in the open rather than one of these, the McLaren Speedtail remains a sought-after collector’s item valued at a couple of million dollars. And if you really want to write your name on the dotted line and park this one in your garage, then you should do just that.
After all, we only live once, don’t we? But how much does this particular McLaren Speedtail actually cost? Well, at the time of writing, the vendor had it advertised on social media for $2,899,900. And that’s a lot more than what these things usually retail for, but then again, the machine in question does have only 54 miles under its belt.
So, if you can afford to fork out almost $3 million on this McLaren Speedtail , then you should definitely reach out to the vendor. But if money were indeed the least of your worries, would you spend the aforementioned sum on this electrified ride? Feel free to drop a line (or more) below and tell us all about it. 2026 SEMA Show • Nissan Seeks Adventures at 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas With Frontier, Pathfinder, Armada Concepts
1935 Cadillac V12 Is One of Two Existing Stationary Coupes, a Forklift Tows It out of the Garage
97 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's (2020)
The thirties were probably not the greatest years to be alive – not by today’s standards, anyway – but one thing that decade has over everything that came after it was carmaking craftsmanship. And nothing would illustrate that level of excellence like a Cadillac (what with it being the Standard of the World and all). Like, say, a one-of-two Stationary Coupe. With a V12 in it. And a manual.
Alright, that last detail might just be a bit of a far-fetched pitch on my behalf, since automatic transmissions (incidentally, introduced by GM in mass production on Oldsmobiles) only came out in 1940. But everything else is just jaw-dropping. What else would you expect from a one-in-eight unicorns?
No, I didn’t lose count. The car in this story is both. When it was new, in 1934 (as a 1935 model year – the detail is crucial, as you’re about to find out immediately), this Stationary Coupe V12 saw a production run of a grand eight units. Come the 2020s, and only two are know to have made it to the present day.
Why is it so important that it was made in 1934 for the next-year lineup, since this has been a norm in the industry for ages? Well, that’s the key to the whole mystery: this norm was generalized in 1935, for the 1936 model year, by Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The president of the United States of Automobile at the time, by the way.
Photo: RM Sotheby's (2020) So, this Cadillac was made a year before that order. Which means the man who ordered it wasn’t just filthy rich, but also very well connected to the powers that be at GM. More on that in a minute. Let’s see what’s what about it before I tell you who the man was.
For 1935, Cadillac built a grand total of 3,636 cars. The overwhelming majority were V8s (3,209 units), leaving the remaining 427 to be split into 377 V12s and a meager 50 V16s. In case you’ve forgotten, Cadillac was about 95 years ahead of Bugatti in putting a V16 motor in a car. Back then, the GM division took its motto to heart, and really set the pace for the auto industry, as the gold Standard of the World.
Nothing illustrates the sheer, unapologetic excess of post-Depression 1930s American luxury better than classic-era Detroit coachbuilding logic. At a time when millions of citizens struggled to mnake ends meet from one paycheck to the next (if they had one), Cadillac happily took a massive 146-inch wheelbase—a footprint long enough to carry a 7-passenger limousine—and draped it in sweeping sheet metal just to coddle a 2+2 coupe whose trunk was marginally larger than its own covered spare tire.
Photo: RM Sotheby's (2020) That magnificent disregard for practicality shines brightly in the private museum of renowned Canadian collector Steve Plunkett in London, Ontario. When Chicago-based YouTuber Lou Costabile visited Plunkett's estate in September of this year, he saw an automotive unicorn. The 1935 Cadillac Series 40 V12 Fleetwood Stationary Coupe.
Despite its curious name, a Stationary Coupe was never meant to sit still inside a climate-controlled garage. In Fleetwood body nomenclature, the term designated a formal two-door coupe fitted with a fixed, non-folding metal roof and a raked V-shaped windshield, separating it from open convertible coupes. Produced across four model years between 1934 and 1937 as Fleetwood Style 5776, this body saw just 45 total units built across all series.
Of those 45 hand-crafted coupes constructed from 1934 through 1937, only half a dozen carried the lowly (by Cadillac standards) V8 engines, all built during the 1934 season, while the remaining 39 housed 12-cylinder or 16-cylinder powerplants. A dozen rode on the V16 chassis—five in 1934, two in 1935, one in 1936, and four in 1937—leaving 27 V12 examples across the four-year run.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Every Stationary Coupe was a highway leviathan in dimensions and curb weight. While V16 versions stretched across a 154-inch wheelbase, the V8 and V12 coupes shared a 146-inch span, measuring 227.5 inches overall on 17-inch wheels and weighing 5,520 or 5,720 pounds (the latter in V12 trim). Buyers could pair the body with a 353-cubic-inch, 130-horsepower Series 30 V8, a 368-cubic-inch, 150-horsepower Series 40 V12, or a 452-cubic-inch, 185-horsepower Series 60 V16.
Such exclusivity carried a breathtaking price tag in 1935. The V12 Stationary Coupe commanded 4,595 dollars new, while the V8 version listed at 3,895 dollars. For perspective, a 1935 Chevrolet Standard started at 500 dollars, and the Coupe cost 522 dollars. When gasoline sold for 10 to 19 cents per gallon and average US household income sat at 1,600 dollars annually, it’s no wonder this Cadillac wasn’t exactly flooding dealerships.
Stamped with Engine Number 4100743 and Body Number 23, Plunkett's coupe still retains a copy of its original factory build sheet. The document shows the car was shipped to Cadillac's Cleveland branch for VIP delivery directly to a "Mr. Prentis," bypassing any dealer in order to get to the owner before by December 31, 1934. Historians link that order to wealthy Cleveland industrialist and philanthropist Francis Fleury Prentiss, whose surname was frequently spelled Prentis in period correspondence.
Photo: RM Sotheby's (2020) The name is virtually unknown today, but he kept Detroit rolling in the first decades of the 20th century. Literally. His companies, Cleveland Graphite Bronze Co., and Cleveland Twist Drill Co., were manufacturing engine bearings and bushings, as well as the tooling required to machine the engines and other precision components. Indeed, GM had every reason to skip any and all middlemen to fulfill this request.
According to that build sheet, the coupe left Detroit finished entirely in sinister black, covering the body, chassis, wheel discs, and even the tires, while carrying factory antifreeze and a Goddess hood mascot. Revered California Cadillac dealer LaRue Thomas preserved the car inside his famous Los Angeles collection for decades until its dissipation in 1993. In 2007, enthusiast David Kane acquired the partially restored coupe and completed its dark blue paintwork and mechanical rebuild.
Kane overhauled the generator, starter, water pump, and fuel pump, installed a new exhaust system, and repaired the radiator with fresh hoses and clamps. Certified as a Classic Car Club of America Full Classic, the coupe sold at RM Sotheby's Hershey auction in October 2018 for 203,500 dollars to Plunkett ($185,000 hammer price).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile After mild cosmetic freshening, it won the Chairman's Choice award at the 2019 Greenwich Concours d'Elegance before going unsold at RM Sotheby's 2020 Arizona auction.
Keeping the coupe after 2020, Plunkett enhanced its teardrop silhouette by installing period-correct rear fender skirts—called wheel shields in the 1930s—over the red-accented wheels and wide whitewalls. Up front, heart-curved fenders frame bullet headlamps, a V12 Fleetwood grille emblem, and a single-bar bumper. Out back, sculpted pods hold real glass taillight lenses beside a decklid whose trunk barely fits the covered spare tire, leaving minimal luggage space.
Swinging open the rear-hinged suicide doors reveals why trunk space vanished: behind the cozy gray broadcloth front bench sits a generous rear compartment housing a pair of fold-down auxiliary jump seats and dual wood-trimmed cabinets. Ahead of the Fleetwood banjo steering wheel, the 120-mph AC speedometer features a frozen main odometer reading 649 miles in 2018, 2020, and September 2026, while its working trip odometer still logs mileage.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile One detail that might not be immediately observed, although it is sitting in plain sight, is the turn signal stalk on the left side of the column. It looks impeccably correct, doesn’t it? It’s a perfectly executed after-market addition – Steve saw to it. it perfectly mimics the brightness and contours and overall expensive feel of the rest of the instrumentation - note the Jaeger Magnetric (with an “R”) clock on the far left of the cluster.
Raising both louvered hood sides exposes the 368-cubic-inch, 45-degree overhead-valve V-12, rated by Plunkett at 135 horsepower, though period catalogs advertised 150 horsepower at 3,600 rpm. Styled like sculpture, the engine hides its wiring inside the center valley beneath a beautiful cover, perfectly matching the valve covers and porcelainized manifolds, or the fluted radiator hoses.
The art exhibition feel of the engine bay continues with the twin updraft carburetors, the optional oil filter, the air-cooled generator that also powers the water pump, and twin bugle horns. And no, the water pump isn’t electric – there’s a drive shaft coming out the back of the generator that makes the pump work.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Technical sophistication abounds underneath, including vacuum-assisted mechanical power brakes introduced in 1930, Cadillac's pioneering automatic choke paired with a manual starter choke, and a 3-speed synchromesh transmission, which the marque invented in 1928.
Powered by a 6-volt, 800-cranking-amp Optima battery (that, according to Steve, may last up to 14 years in his 1930s-era cars), the V12 whispers down Ontario roads while Plunkett works the extra-long shifter lever (we can safely call it a shift pole), carefully minding the unprotected reverse gate located straight up from first gear.
Even getting the coupe out of its spotless showroom involves clever engineering. Because cold 1930s engines (V12s or not) spit black carbon water from their tailpipes and smoke up indoor walls, Plunkett fabricated a custom steel attachment for his forklift that hooks beneath the front axle, towing the 2.6-ton classic outside before turning the key. It is a fittingly thorough ritual for keeping one of the rarest pre-war Cadillacs ready for the open road.

2026 SEMA Show • This Batmobile-Looking Lamborghini Temerario Is on Display at SEMA
4 New Hot Wheels Coming to the Pantone Series Soon
13 photos
Photo: THunted
Two years ago, I would watch three to four new movies every week. Right now, life is so hectic that I’ve only seen less than one a month in 2026. I’m ecstatic about going to Godzilla Minus Zero soon and I hope it won’t be disappointing. Also, Dune is coming up next month!
Even though I haven’t been able to indulge in one of my favorite pastimes, I’ve been putting together a long list of titles I can follow once I move into a new home. It involves mostly going back to the ‘70s and ‘80s, while mixing in plenty of international titles while I’m at it. And I’m definitely adding Herbie to my list, even though I’ve just recently discovered the series.
It was a sort of reverse Pop Culture experience, as I learned through a preview of Mattel’s premium series. For a while, I thought the 4-car set might have been the work of a custom artist, or even worse (something created after a prompt). But today, one of my dealers posted some photos of the four Volkswagen models, effectively removing the remaining doubt I was struggling with.
I’m not here to talk about Herbie though, and I don’t plan to spend too much time with the Mazda RX-7 either. All you need to know is that Jun Imai’s is getting a ZAMAC release for next year’s Nightspeed mini-series (Walmart Exclusive) and the whole thing is kind of annoying to me as a Premium version of this car hasn’t showed up yet.
I’m not saying everything is perfect with the second and third generation RX-7 castings, but we still have quite a few more options to choose from there. And now, let’s focus on what’s coming to the Silver Series Pantone theme in 2027. It all started this year with three sets and a total of 18 collectibles.
Well, I’ve heard rumors that Mix 3 will be adding an unnumbered, Chase version of the '64 Corvette Sting Ray but we’ll have to wait a while longer to see if that’s true or not (it probably is). The first preview photos for 2027 will certainly lead to mixed feelings, as two of the four castings are original Hot Wheels designs.
That’s one to throw a 50th anniversary party for Larry Wood’s Second Wind. We saw a SpongeBob-themed one in 2024, and it was one of just three variations to show up in toy stores in this century. Yes, you heard that right: Mattel mainly marketed it between 1977 and 1986, with two further iterations before the turn of the millennium.
Does that mean this blue version is here to send it into retirement or to revive it for a few more years? Time will tell. Super Blitzen is a bit more interesting to me, as it’s basically a futuristic version of a touring car. Ryu Asada created it for the 2011 New Models series, and it has been missing in action since 2021.
Even though it has never been part of the Silver Series before, you will find two special ID variations if you’re into that sort of stuff. As far as I can tell, the only one of the four cars that will have a metal base is the '91 Nissan Sentra SE-R. It debuted in the 2022 Japanese Tuners Collector Set and has only had premium releases since (except for this year’s Compact Kings/Silver Series model).
The paint job is anything but exciting, which means most collectors might just focus on the Porsche 918 Spyder instead (if we can find one in the first place). It will be the third Porsche entry in the Pantone series.
Everyone is bound to be happy that Mattel hasn’t axed the project yet, as the previous three variations were all part of 20-Packs. The casting is almost a decade old at this point, so it’s not what I’d call perfect. However, I’m certain Ronald Wong has it on his “To Do” list for the near future: a Premium take would certainly start a treasure hunt!

Chevy Corvette Fighters Edition Is a C8 on Steroids That Comes From Japan With Lots of Love
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato
The C8-generation Chevrolet Corvette keeps making headlines almost seven years after it entered production, and one of the latest to have crossed our screens is pictured in the gallery below.
It is called the Fighters Edition, and lives in the Land of the Rising Sun. And as you can likely tell, it is not a special model signed by the bowtie brand’s local arm and aimed at the local market exclusively, because this thing has come directly from a portfolio of a renowned Japanese tuner. We are talking about Liberty Walk, and as you likely recall, this company has already left its mark on other C8 cars over the years.
Presented during a special event, as far as we can tell, and breathing the same air as some fighter jets, as well as other cool projects signed by this tuner, the Chevrolet Corvette Fighters Edition stands out from the crowd immediately due to its exterior design, which comprises a special livery in gray, with some red accents here and there, a few black details, and the usual decals that one would expect from a Liberty Walk build.
Mind you, this thing would not be a real Liberty Walk project if it weren’t for the widebody kit, which comprises the very fat wheel arch extensions at the front and rear. The OEM bumper was also enlarged in order to fit the wide design of the car, and it also features a very sharp-looking apron attached to it. It appears that the front hood has been retained, but the changes continue further back, where this thing sports redesigned side skirts that are also on the fat side of things.
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato The back end of this special Chevrolet Corvette from the C8 generation is partially visible in one of the pictures that Liberty Walk’s founder recently shared on social media with his 1.7-million followers, but we do not need more to tell that the diffuser, which is very large, has come directly from this tuner’s shelves, and so has the massive wing attached to the rear deck, which contributes to the motorsport vibe that this build sends from all angles.
As it is common with projects coming from this company, the Chevy Corvette in question also sits a lot closer to the asphalt compared to the stock one, which inevitably tells us that Liberty Walk has also left its mark on the suspension. And chances are it is an air adjustable setup that lowers and raises the body at the push of a button. Or is that at the flick of a switch? Either way, this thing definitely looks like it was born to feast on apexes.
But don’t let the motorsport-like look trick you into thinking that it is not street legal anymore, because it is. It’s just a tuned C8 Chevrolet Corvette , one that also features new wheels. The alloys are slimmer at the front and wider at the rear, from what we can tell. They have a black look, were supposedly wrapped in sticky tires for enhanced traction during the corner-feasting stunts, and they spin around the yellow brake calipers.
The interior of this machine is only partially visible by zooming in through the windows in certain pictures, and it looks like it sports red leather upholstery and plenty of black accents. And if we didn’t know better, we’d say that Liberty Walk has also left its mark on the cockpit. However, it hasn’t, because this tuner usually draws the line after modifying a car’s exterior. So, unless a different company was involved in the aftermarket work, then the cabin remains fully OEM.
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato And guess what? The same applies to the powertrain, too, because the tuner is not famously known for boosting the oomph of its builds. Liberty Walk hasn’t had much to say about this project, and he hasn’t mentioned the specification of the pictured Chevrolet Corvette either. However, chances are we are looking at the Stingray, which features a 6.2-liter V8 engine making up to 495 hp (502 ps/369 kW) in the pre-facelifted iteration.
This model needs 2.9 seconds to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill, and takes a little over 11 seconds to complete the standing quarter mile. As for its successor, it now uses an LS6. The V8 has a 6.7-liter displacement, and pumps out 535 hp (542 ps/399 kW), dropping the 0-60 mph sprint time by one-tenth of a second compared to the older iteration to 2.8 seconds, albeit with the optional Z51 Performance Pack. The 1/4-mile is an 11-second affair, with an exit speed of 124 mph (200 kph), and the top speed is 200+ mph (322+ kph).
Now, this tuned Chevrolet Corvette that lives in Japan and had its pictures taken at the Misawa Air Base definitely stands out for all the right reasons, this writer believes, but do you dig the makeover? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Wataru Kato (@libertywalkkato)
